title: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is at least obvious, with the Liesegang phenomenon in view, that we have no right to _assume_ that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily bound up with, and indubitably brought about by, a periodic recurrence of particular _external_ conditions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IX, “On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons”; topic “Liesegang rings and growth zones”. Scope: fish scales and otoliths, bones, starch grains and other concentrically zoned organic structures

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch09-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The modest claim rejects necessity rather than all environmental control, so a single well-supported endogenous counterexample is informative. Open sclerochronology and environmental series can test several systems, though not the entire heterogeneous scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For dated growth-zone series, test whether increments align reliably with independent seasonal or diel markers and compare externally forced versus endogenous reaction-diffusion models. Finding internally generated periodicity or poor alignment would refute the assumption that visible rings necessarily record external cycles.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Different structures have different ring-forming mechanisms.

Environmental covariates and internal rhythms can be correlated.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The empirical content is that rhythmic zones are not necessarily calendars, and known-age hard parts can supply mismatches or matches. Increment series are public but scattered across PANGAEA deposits and papers, and they cover a subset of the structures named. Because the claim is a prohibition on assuming an external cause, one well-documented endogenous case is informative, while entrainment keeps many individual series ambiguous.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains with known-age or known-environment series, test whether zone counts match day, season or other external periods. Zones that form without a matching external cycle support the claim that periodicity need not be external; a universal match would refute that caution.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Starch grains and most bones are poorly represented next to commercial fish otoliths and bivalve or coral bands.

An endogenous oscillator can still lock to an external cycle, so agreement does not prove external cause.
